Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
Tariq was fifty-four when he finally walked into the clinic, but the memory that brought him there lived in a cramped maintenance closet of his former apartment complex two years prior. He had gone down to report a faulty breaker, only to find the building’s night security guard waiting inside. The man had turned the lock from the inside, pinned him against the concrete wall, and stripped away his dignity while the emergency sirens began to wail through the parking structure. The guttural rush of an ambulance arriving that night became the opening note of his life afterward. He had come to believe the event happened because of the way he acted, because he had answered the call, because he had walked into the closet, because he had hesitated. He was certain the system had abandoned him, that his suffering was a profound injustice left to fester without accountability. In the months that followed, Tariq’s world shrank. He stopped driving past the complex. Whenever a siren cut through the air, even from three blocks away, his heart would hammer against his ribs, his breath shallowing as if the maintenance door were closing again. He often found himself reacting as though the threat were present, jumping at the sudden beep of a microwave or the heavy footsteps of a delivery driver. He began mapping his day by safe zones. He only felt secure in his own bathroom, at his kitchen table, and in the corner of his office where he could see every exit. His scanning became automatic. He would walk into a room and immediately note the angles of the doorways, the placement of the staff, the color of the uniforms. He avoided any man who approached him alone, finding an excuse to step out of the elevator or take a different route to the break room. When a client wore a navy blazer that resembled a service jacket, Tariq would abruptly end the call. He told himself he would never be able to feel normal emotions again; his chest felt sealed shut, a permanent dullness where grief, joy, or even simple relief used to live. At the tech campus where he worked as a software engineer, the avoidance took on a specific shape. He requested a desk in the far west wing, far from the building’s central security checkpoint. During sprint planning meetings, he kept his monitor angled toward the wall and his hands folded tightly in his lap, his eyes constantly tracking the door and the shift of weight among the developers. He never went to the on-site IT help desk, and he made sure to leave the building if a patrol of private security contractors wearing tactical vests and carrying radios approached his floor. He avoided military and police uniforms or the sight of weapons entirely, rerouting his commute to bypass the transit hub where officers regularly patrolled. Instead, he submitted tickets remotely, waiting until his screen flickered with a confirmation that the work would be done by someone else. The open-plan environment forced him to navigate a landscape of unspoken threats. A male colleague once patted his shoulder after a successful deployment, and Tariq had frozen, his pulse spiking until the man moved away. He didn’t confront it. He just started wearing noise-canceling headphones and keeping his office door propped open with a wooden block. The emotional numbness and the exhaustion of constant scanning coexisted in his daily life until the quiet he had constructed finally felt heavier than the wailing sirens. He stopped attending team lunches. He let his phone ring past the second time. He came to the clinic because the isolation he had maintained felt unsustainable. He was most afraid that the numbness would never lift, that he would spend the rest of his life walking through rooms calculating escape routes while his own life paused. What he hoped for, quietly, was simply to hear a siren without his breath catching, to sit in a chair with a male supervisor without bracing for impact, and to wake up one morning and feel something that wasn’t measured in survival.
